2.text: The wooden fire-tool has already been described. The board in which

3.text: the drill revolves is roughly shaped into a human form. Usually it represents

4.text: only a head and shoulders, though legs are sometimes added (Fig. 246).

5.text: Eyes, nose, and mouth are indicated by cuts of appropriate form and position.

6.text: At every sacrifice its mouth is greased with tallow or with the marrow of

7.text: bones. This image is called “reindeer fire-tool” (in Chukchee, g̣ɪˊrg̣ɪr, pl.,

9.text: connection with the herd. The holes made by drilling are considered the

10.text: eyes of the fire-board; and the squeaking noise produced by

11.text: the drilling, its voice. In those camps where the wooden

12.text: fire-tool is still daily employed for lighting fires, the

13.text: sacred fire-boards are often reserved for ceremonials, and

14.text: for regular use a substitute is made (Fig. 247). Sometimes

15.text: this is merely a board; in other cases it is given the

16.text: shape of a human figure, and after several years’ use it
16.note: Curly apostrophe confirmed at 2x (zoom2-16p52-100.png), per §1 book-wide curly-quote convention.

17.text: is laid aside with other fire-boards. Its sacredness is

18.text: derived from its daily connection with the fire of the hearth.

19.text: Many families have several fire-boards. Some of them are comparatively

20.text: new; others, inherited from preceding generations, are often quite ancient.

21.text: Each is associated with the ownership of a certain portion of the herd, marked

22.text: with its own brand. These brands pass with the sacred fire-board from generation

23.text: to generation. Each boy born to the family is given, when he is four or five
